beats.headline: Why does Kafka run on a 6GB heap with 128GB of RAM?
beats.subline: It is not a memory leak—it is a deliberate design to bypass the JVM entirely.
beats.narration: Why does Kafka run on a tiny 6GB heap even on massive servers? It is not a bug. It is a design choice to let the Linux kernel handle the heavy lifting.

beats.title: The Page Cache Strategy
beats.subtitle: Bypassing the JVM for raw speed
beats.narration: Kafka offloads data caching to the OS Page Cache. This prevents double-caching and keeps your data warm in RAM even if the broker JVM restarts, completely avoiding massive GC pauses.

beats.title: Log Segment Architecture

steps.explanation: Immutable segments roll at 1GB. Deleting old data is just an un-link operation.
Maps offsets to physical file positions. Only 8 bytes per entry.

beats.narration: Kafka splits partitions into rolling log segments. The sparse index maps offsets to byte positions, allowing binary search lookups without loading the entire file into memory.

beats.title: Inspecting Partition State
beats.caption: Verify ISR and Leader status
beats.narration: Use the CLI to check your ISR—the In-Sync Replicas. If a follower lags behind, it gets kicked out of the ISR to prevent data loss during leader elections.

beats.headline: Why does TLS encryption cripple Kafka throughput?
beats.subline: It breaks the zero-copy pipeline that gives Kafka its speed.
beats.narration: Kafka is fast because it uses zero-copy. But turn on TLS, and that performance advantage often vanishes. Here is why your encryption settings matter.

beats.title: The Zero-Copy Pipeline
beats.subtitle: Direct memory transfer to NIC
beats.narration: With zero-copy, data moves from the Page Cache directly to the NIC via DMA. It never touches the JVM heap, saving CPU cycles and memory bandwidth.

beats.title: FileChannel.transferTo()

steps.explanation: Delegates to the OS sendfile system call to bypass user-space buffers.

beats.narration: This method triggers the sendfile system call. It tells the kernel to pull bytes from the page cache and push them to the socket buffer directly.

beats.title: Plaintext vs. TLS Performance
beats.narration: TLS requires encryption in user-space. This forces data to copy into the JVM, killing the zero-copy benefit. Always benchmark your CPU usage after enabling TLS.

beats.headline: What happens when a partition leader crashes?
beats.subline: Data is not lost if you understand the High Watermark.
beats.narration: When a leader crashes, how does Kafka ensure no data is lost? It relies on the In-Sync Replicas set and the High Watermark.

beats.title: Replication Flow
beats.subtitle: LEO, HW, and ISR
beats.narration: The High Watermark is the minimum LEO across the ISR. Consumers only see records up to this point, ensuring they never read uncommitted data.

beats.title: Leader Election Rules
beats.caption: Why unclean leader election is dangerous

lines.text: # Keep this false for transactional data!

beats.narration: Never enable unclean leader election for financial data. It allows lagging followers to become leaders, which guarantees data loss for any records not yet replicated.

beats.title: Clean vs. Unclean Election
beats.narration: Clean election is the default. It waits for an ISR member to take over. Unclean election prioritizes uptime over consistency, which is usually a bad trade.

beats.headline: Why did Kafka finally kill ZooKeeper?
beats.subline: Metadata scaling was the bottleneck holding back massive clusters.
beats.narration: ZooKeeper was a bottleneck for large clusters. Kafka 4.0 finally killed it with KRaft. Here is why the new metadata architecture is a game changer.

beats.title: KRaft Architecture
beats.subtitle: Metadata as an event stream
beats.narration: KRaft stores metadata in an internal Kafka topic. Controllers use Raft for consensus, making metadata updates fast, consistent, and scalable to hundreds of thousands of partitions.

beats.title: KRaft Configuration
beats.caption: Setting up the controller quorum
beats.narration: In KRaft mode, nodes act as both brokers and controllers. You define the quorum voters directly in your config, removing the need for a separate ZK cluster.

beats.title: ZooKeeper vs. KRaft
beats.narration: ZooKeeper was a separate system to manage. KRaft brings metadata into Kafka itself, simplifying operations and drastically improving failover speed from minutes to milliseconds.
